lead: A state function depends only on where the system is, not on how it got there. Pressure, volume and internal energy are state functions. Work and heat are path functions: their values depend on the route between the same two states. Engineers use this split to compute work in pistons, compressors and turbines, and to judge how close a process comes to the reversible ideal. Q and W both change with the path, yet the first law says their difference Q − W is the same for every path.
prereq: You need 1.1 for system, boundary and properties.

sections.h3: State functions, path functions and differentials

blocks.text: A state function has a fixed value once the state is fixed by properties such as P, V and T. Its value does not depend on history. Some syllabi call it a point function because it belongs to one point on a property diagram. Pressure P, volume V, temperature T and internal energy U are state functions. The change ΔU = U₂ − U₁ depends only on the two end states.

A path function depends on the route between the states. Work W and heat Q are path functions. They are energy in transit across the boundary, not stored properties; see 1.3. A small amount of work is written δW and a small amount of heat as δQ. The symbol δ is used because there is no function W(P,V) or Q(P,V) whose difference gives δW or δQ. Write W for total work, not ΔW.

blocks.where: X is any state function; ∮ means integration around a closed path that returns to the same state; dX is an exact differential.

blocks.text: dX = M(x, y) dx + N(x, y) dy is exact when ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x
blocks.where: M and N are functions of x and y; ∂M/∂y is the partial derivative of M with respect to y; ∂M/∂y is taken with x held fixed and ∂N/∂x with y held fixed. Some syllabi call this the exactness (Euler) test.

blocks.text: Try the test on an ideal gas, with T and V as the two variables. Internal energy gives dU = C<sub>v</sub> dT + 0·dV: here ∂C<sub>v</sub>/∂V = 0 and ∂(0)/∂T = 0, so dU is exact. Reversible work gives δW = P dV = 0·dT + (RT/V) dV: now ∂(0)/∂V = 0 but ∂(RT/V)/∂T = R/V, which is not zero, so δW is inexact. The test proves what the next section shows with areas.

items: Exact differential: value depends only on endpoints; the quantity is a state function.
Inexact differential: value depends on the path; the quantity is a path function such as W or Q.
For a state function, the cyclic integral is zero. For work, ∮ δW is not zero in general.

blocks.text: A reversible process is an ideal limit. The system moves through a quasi-static path: it stays infinitesimally close to equilibrium, so P and T are nearly uniform inside it. There is no friction and no finite driving force. The external pressure differs from the system pressure by only dP, and the external temperature differs from the system temperature by only dT. An infinitesimal change in the driving force can reverse the direction.

Sign rule for the whole unit: W is work done by the system and Q is heat added to it, so the first law reads ΔU = Q − W (set out in work and heat). For a reversible expansion, the external pressure equals the system pressure at every step. The work done by the gas is the area under the P–V curve: W = ∫ P dV. This path can be drawn on a P–V diagram because P is defined at each step. Reversible paths are useful limits: they give the maximum work in expansion and the minimum work in compression.

blocks.where: δW is small work done by the system in J; P<sub>ext</sub> is the external pressure in Pa or kPa; dV is the small volume change in m³ or L. For a reversible path, P<sub>ext</sub> = P, the system pressure.

blocks.text: Real processes are irreversible to some degree. Friction, stirring and finite temperature differences add dissipation. A reversible process is not a claim that real equipment is reversible; it is a benchmark for calculations and for the second-law limits studied later.

sections.h3: Irreversible processes and the same endpoints

blocks.text: An irreversible process cannot be reversed by an infinitesimal change. It has finite driving forces, gradients or friction, and reversing it leaves a net change in the surroundings. Common examples are sudden expansion of a gas, paddle-wheel stirring of a liquid, and heat transfer across a finite temperature difference.

In a sudden expansion, the gas pushes a piston against a finite external pressure. The work is W = P<sub>ext</sub>(V₂ − V₁), not ∫ P dV, because the gas pressure inside may not be uniform and is not equal to P<sub>ext</sub>. In free expansion into vacuum, P<sub>ext</sub> = 0, so the work is zero. Stirring puts work into the liquid and raises its temperature; the liquid cannot spontaneously turn that heat back into shaft work.

The same two end states can give different work along different paths. On a P–V plot, work done by the gas is the area under the path. Two routes between the same endpoints have different areas, so W differs. This is the clearest proof that work is a path function, not a state function.

blocks.where: W is work done by the gas in J; P is absolute pressure in Pa or kPa; V is volume in m³ or L. Use consistent units; 1 kPa·L = 1 J.

examples.question: A gas changes from A (P = 3 kPa, V = 1 L) to B (P = 1 kPa, V = 3 L) by two slow (quasi-static) paths, each made of two straight segments on the P–V plot. Path A passes through (2 L, 1.5 kPa); path B passes through (2 L, 2 kPa). Because both paths are quasi-static, the gas pressure is defined at every step and the work equals the area under each path. Compute the work done by the gas along each path. Use 1 kPa·L = 1 J.
steps: For a straight segment on a P–V plot, area = average pressure × volume change = 0.5(P₁ + P₂)(V₂ − V₁).
The endpoints are the same, but W<sub>A</sub> ≠ W<sub>B</sub>. Work is a path function.
examples.answer: Work along path A is 3.5 J and along path B is 4.0 J; the same endpoints give different work, so work is a path function.

traps: Treating work as a state function because a reversible path lets you calculate it from P and V. Reversible only means P is defined along the path; it does not make work path-independent.
Thinking all reversible paths between two states give the same work. Different reversible P–V routes have different areas under them.
Writing dW or ΔW for a small or total amount of work. Use δW for a small path-dependent amount and W for total work.
Using W = ∫ P dV for an irreversible sudden expansion. Use W = P<sub>ext</sub>(V₂ − V₁) when P<sub>ext</sub> is fixed and finite, and remember P<sub>ext</sub> may not equal the gas pressure.
Mixing up exact and inexact differentials: ∮ dX = 0 for a state function X, but ∮ δW is generally not zero.

quiz.q: Define a state function and a path function. Give one example of each.
quiz.a: A state function depends only on the state, not the path; examples are P, V, U. A path function depends on the route; examples are W and Q.

quiz.q: Why is work a path function even when both paths are reversible?
quiz.a: For a reversible path, W = ∫P dV, which is the area under the P–V curve. Different reversible routes between the same endpoints have different areas, so W differs.

quiz.q: A gas expands at a constant 100 kPa from 2 L to 5 L. Find the work done by the gas. Use 1 kPa·L = 1 J.

Two paths between the same states have W<sub>A</sub> = 5 J and W<sub>B</sub> = 8 J, with W the work done by the system and ΔU = Q − W. The change in internal energy is the same. Find Q<sub>B</sub> − Q<sub>A</sub>.
quiz.a: Q = ΔU + W for each path, and ΔU is the same, so Q<sub>B</sub> − Q<sub>A</sub> = W<sub>B</sub> − W<sub>A</sub> = 8 − 5 = 3 J. Path B takes in 3 J more heat because it does 3 J more work.

quiz.q: What is ∮ dX for a state function X around a closed path?
quiz.a: It is zero, because X returns to its starting value.

quiz.q: State two conditions that make a process reversible.
quiz.a: The process is quasi-static with infinitesimal driving forces, and there is no friction or dissipation. The system and surroundings can then be restored by an infinitesimal change.

quiz.q: A student says all reversible paths between two states give the same work. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: The statement is false. Reversible means the path is well-defined so W = ∫P dV can be used, but different reversible P–V routes have different areas under them. Work remains path-dependent.

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant design, the gap between a real compressor and an ideal reversible one is a measure of lost work, which the second law puts a number on. Process simulators build P–V and T–s paths to estimate power. The same exactness test returns in the Maxwell relations of thermodynamic property relations. Search for quasi-static process, path function on a P–V diagram and exact differential in thermodynamics.
